intro: IEC 62351 adds security to grid protocols that were built without it. Part 3 wraps a TCP protocol, such as IEC 104 between a control center and its substations, in TLS, the same protection that secure websites use. First comes the handshake. Both sides show a certificate, a signed digital ID card in the X.509 format, issued by a CA (certificate authority) they both trust. After the handshake, every byte is encrypted and protected against change. A device without a valid certificate cannot even start.
plain: Power grids are run from control rooms that send commands to substations, and many of those links were built with no protection at all. This standard adds it. Before they talk, both sides show a digital ID card signed by an authority they both trust, like a staff badge checked at the door. After that, everything they say travels in a sealed envelope that nobody else can read or change without being noticed.

connect.title: Open a connection
connect.text: SCADA, the control center's system, opens a TCP connection to the RTU (remote terminal unit), the control box in the substation. It uses port 19998, the port for IEC 104 over TLS. Plain IEC 104 uses 2404.

hello.title: Say hello
hello.text: Both sides send 32 random bytes. They agree on the TLS version and a cipher suite: a set of methods that says how the keys are made, which signatures count and how the data is encrypted.

rtu-proof.title: The RTU proves itself
rtu-proof.text: The RTU sends its certificate. It also signs its half of the key exchange with its private key: the secret that belongs to that certificate and never leaves the RTU. Then it asks SCADA for a certificate from the CA it trusts. SCADA checks the RTU's certificate: signed by the utility's CA, not expired, not revoked (canceled before its end date).

scada-proof.title: SCADA proves itself
scada-proof.text: SCADA sends its certificate and signs everything said so far. Both sides compute the same keys and turn on encryption. The first encrypted message, Finished, proves that nobody changed the handshake. With IEC 62351-8, the certificate can also name SCADA's role, such as OPERATOR. The RTU checks that role before it accepts a command.

data.title: IEC 104 inside TLS
data.text: The IEC 104 messages now travel as before: STARTDT (start data transfer), the interrogation (a request for all current values) and the breaker trip. Each one travels inside an encrypted TLS record. Someone who captures the traffic sees only the record headers and their lengths.

reject.title: An expired certificate
reject.text: A maintenance laptop tries to connect. Its certificate expired on 31 October. The RTU stops the handshake with a fatal alert, an error message that ends the connection, and logs the attempt. It never accepts a single IEC 104 byte from the laptop.

frames.tcp: Open a TCP connection to port 19998
frames.client-hello: Hello: I speak TLS 1.2, with these cipher suites
frames.cert-request: Now show me yours, from Grid CA
frames.laptop-hello: Hello, here is my certificate: CN=ENG-LAPTOP-03

notes.tcp: Plain TCP. The RTU accepts the connection and waits for a TLS ClientHello. Anything else ends the connection.
notes.server-cert: Two records. Certificate carries the RTU's X.509 certificate and any CA certificates above it in the chain, about 1 kB. In TLS 1.2, anyone can read it. ServerKeyExchange carries the RTU's elliptic-curve (ECDHE) public key for this session, signed with the private key of that certificate.
notes.client-cert: Three records. Certificate: SCADA's own X.509 certificate. ClientKeyExchange: its ECDHE public key. CertificateVerify: a signature over every handshake message so far, made with SCADA's private key. A copied certificate without its key cannot make this signature.
notes.laptop-hello: The same handshake as above, shortened: TCP, ClientHello, the RTU's certificate and request, then the laptop's certificate. The RTU checks its dates against its own clock and finds Not After: 31 October 2026.

rec-handshake.name: Content type
rec-handshake.note: 0x16 = 22: a handshake message, not encrypted yet.

hs-client-hello.name: ClientHello
hs-client-hello.note: Handshake type 1: the client's first message.

client-version.name: Highest version
client-version.note: TLS 1.2 is the highest version SCADA offers.

client-random.name: Client random
client-random.note: 32 random bytes. Both randoms go into the session keys, so every session gets new keys.

no-session.name: Session ID
no-session.note: Length 0: a new session, nothing to resume.

suites.name: Cipher suites
suites.note: Two: 0xC02B (ECDHE key exchange, ECDSA certificates, AES-128-GCM) and 0xC02F (the same with RSA certificates).

groups.name: supported_groups
groups.note: The elliptic curve for the key exchange: secp256r1 (0x0017).

sigalgs.name: signature_algorithms
sigalgs.note: The signatures SCADA can check: RSA with SHA-256 (0x0401) and ECDSA with SHA-256 (0x0403).

ems.name: extended_master_secret
ems.note: Ties the keys to this whole handshake, so the same keys cannot be forced onto another connection (RFC 7627).

reneg.name: renegotiation_info
reneg.note: Makes a later renegotiation safe (RFC 5746). A connection that stays open for months can renew its keys this way.

server-version.name: Version
server-version.note: TLS 1.2: the version both will use.

server-no-session.name: Session ID
server-no-session.note: Length 0: the RTU will not keep this session, so every new connection does the full handshake.

reneg-ok.name: renegotiation_info
reneg-ok.note: The RTU supports safe renegotiation too.

hs-cert-request.name: CertificateRequest
hs-cert-request.note: Handshake type 13: the RTU wants a certificate from SCADA too. IEC 62351-3 requires this check in both directions.

cert-types.name: Certificate types
cert-types.note: One type: 1, a certificate with an RSA key.

cr-sigalgs.name: Signatures
cr-sigalgs.note: The signatures the RTU accepts: 0x0401 and 0x0403.

ca-list.name: CA names
ca-list.note: 40 bytes: the names of the CAs the RTU trusts, here one.

dn-seq.name: Name
dn-seq.note: The name in ASN.1 DER coding, where every part is a tag, a length and a value. 0x30: a sequence of 36 bytes.

dn-o-type.name: O
dn-o-type.note: One part of the name: attribute 2.5.4.10, the organization.

dn-o.name: Grid Co
dn-o.note: Its value, a UTF-8 string (0x0C) of 7 characters.

dn-cn-type.name: CN
dn-cn-type.note: The second part: attribute 2.5.4.3, the common name.

dn-cn.name: Grid CA
dn-cn.note: The CA's name. Only a certificate signed by this CA will do.

hs-done.name: ServerHelloDone
hs-done.note: Handshake type 14: the RTU has said everything.

ccs.name: Change cipher spec
ccs.note: 1: every record after this one is encrypted with the new keys.

rec-40.name: Length
rec-40.note: 40 encrypted bytes follow, not shown: an 8-byte nonce (a number used once), the Finished message (16 bytes) and a 16-byte tag. Finished holds a hash of the whole handshake.

rec-30.name: Length
rec-30.note: 30 encrypted bytes follow, not shown: an 8-byte nonce, the 6 bytes of STARTDT act (68 04 07 00 00 00) and a 16-byte tag that reveals any change.

rec-47.name: Length
rec-47.note: 47 encrypted bytes follow: an 8-byte nonce, the 23-byte M_DP_TB_1 frame (the breaker's new position, with a time stamp) and a 16-byte tag. Only the length shows that something was sent.

rec-alert.name: Content type
rec-alert.note: 0x15 = 21: an alert, in clear text because the handshake never finished.

expired.name: Description 45
expired.note: 0x2D: certificate_expired. A certificate from a CA the RTU does not trust gets 48 (0x30, unknown_ca) instead.

cs-tls.name: TLS
cs-tls.note: The protocol: this suite is one of TLS 1.2's.

cs-ecdhe.name: ECDHE · key exchange
cs-ecdhe.note: Elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman with new keys for every session: a recorded session cannot be read later, even with the certificate's key.

cs-rsa.name: RSA · who proves
cs-rsa.note: The RTU, the server, proves who it is by signing with the RSA key of its certificate.

cs-aes.name: AES_128_GCM · encryption
cs-aes.note: Each record is encrypted with AES and a 128-bit key, and GCM adds a check that nothing was changed.

cs-sha.name: SHA256 · hash
cs-sha.note: The hash used to make the session's keys from the handshake.

facts.standard: IEC 62351-3 (TLS for TCP protocols), with -8 (roles) and -9 (keys and certificates)
facts.between: SCADA ↔ RTU, client ↔ IED: any TCP connection of IEC 104, DNP3 or MMS
facts.transport: TLS 1.2 on TCP 19998 for IEC 104 (19999 for DNP3, 3782 for MMS)
facts.security: X.509 certificates on both sides, checked for issuer, dates and revocation
facts.frames: TLS records: 0x16 handshake, 0x14 change cipher spec, 0x15 alert, 0x17 application data

tips: Certificates expire. Keep a list of every device's Not After date and renew early: when the date passes, the connection simply fails.
The RTU checks dates with its own clock. A clock that falls back to 1970 after a power cut makes every certificate look not yet valid. Set the time before the first connection.

Check revocation too. A stolen laptop's certificate works until the CA revokes it and the RTU reads the new list of revoked certificates (CRL). IEC 62351-9 covers how certificates are issued and revoked.

TLS protects TCP only. GOOSE and Sampled Values travel without IP, so IEC 62351-6 adds an authentication code (a check value made with a secret key) to each of their frames instead, with keys from IEC 62351-9.

playground.file: The laptop's certificate, as openssl prints it (made up, from a test CA). Find out why the RTU refused it.
playground.command: openssl prints a certificate in readable form. Try it on your own devices' certificates.
playground.issuer: Who signed it: Grid CA, the CA the RTU named in its CertificateRequest.
playground.not-after: The last valid moment: 31 October 2026. The lesson takes place on 12 November, so it has expired.
playground.subject: Who it belongs to. An RTU can also check this name against a list of allowed partners.
playground.key-usage: What the key may do. Critical: a device that does not understand this extension must reject the certificate.
playground.client-auth: It may be used by a TLS client, not by a server.
playground.crl: Where the list of revoked certificates (the CRL) is published. The RTU must reach it, or hold a recent copy.
playground.verify: openssl comes to the same verdict as the RTU: error 10, certificate has expired.

anatomy.suite: The name of the cipher suite the RTU chose
